source_refs.note: Applications: a main subheading of 5.7 Archimedes' principle and floatation, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 101-104.

blocks.text: Following are some important applications of Archimedes' principle.
1. Hot-air balloon

The reason why hot-air balloons rise and float in mid-air is because of the density of the hot-air balloon is less than the surrounding air. When the buoyant force of the hot-air balloon is more, it starts to rise. This is done by varying the quantity of hot air in the balloon.

blocks.alt: A hot-air balloon floating in the air: a tall rounded envelope with a dark top, red-orange and yellow zigzag bands round its middle and a dark lower part narrowing to its mouth, with a small basket hanging below on ropes.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.9: Hot-air balloon (original drawing after the photograph printed as the textbook's Figure 5.9).

blocks.text: 2. Wooden block floating on water

A wooden block floats on water. It is because the weight of an equal volume of water is greater than the weight of the block. According to the principle of floatation, a body floats if its displaced water is equal to the weight of the body when it is partially or completely immersed in water.
3. Ships and boats

Ships and boats are designed on the same principle of floatation. They carry passengers and goods over water. It would sink in water if its weight including the weight of its passengers and goods becomes greater than the upthrust of water.

blocks.alt: A large white passenger ship floating on a calm blue sea, seen from above: its bow far away at the upper left and its rounded stern near at the lower right, rows of windows along its side, black-and-white decks stepping round the stern, and a funnel and green sun deck on top.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.10(a): A ship floating over water (original drawing after the photograph printed as the textbook's Figure 5.10(a)).

blocks.text: 4. Submarine
A submarine can travel over as well as under water using the same principle of floatation.

blocks.alt: A yellow submarine seen from the side, with leaders to its labelled parts: the periscope and antenna on top of the tower, the propeller at the back, the sonar at the front and a row of round portholes along the hull.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.10(b): Submarine (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.10(b)).

blocks.text: It floats over water when the weight of water equal to its volume is greater than its weight. Under this condition, it is similar to a ship and remains partially above water level. It has a system of tanks which can be filled with and emptied from seawater. When these tanks are filled with seawater, the weight of the submarine increases. As soon as its weight becomes greater than the upthrust, it dives into water and remains under water. To come up on the surface, the tanks are made empty from seawater.
Example 5.3

An empty meteorological balloon weighs 80 N. It is filled with 10 cubic metres of hydrogen. How much maximum contents the balloon can lift besides its own weight? The density of hydrogen is 0.09 kg m⁻³ and the density of air is 1.3 kg m⁻³.
Given:
Weight of the balloon w = 80 N
Volume of hydrogen V = 10 m³
Density of hydrogen ρ₁ = 0.09 kg m⁻³
Density of air ρ₂ = 1.3 kg m⁻³
Weight of hydrogen w₁ = ?
Weight of the contents w₂ = ?
Upthrust F = Weight of air displaced
= ρ₂gV
= 1.3 kg m⁻³ x 9.8 m s⁻² x 10 m³
Weight of hydrogen w₁ = ρ₁Vg
= 0.09 kg m⁻³ x 10 m³ x 9.8 m s⁻²
Total weight lifted F = w + w₁ + w₂
To lift the contents, the total weight of the balloon should not exceed F.
Thus w + w₁ + w₂ = F
or w₂ = 38 N
Thus, the maximum weight of 41 N can be lifted by the balloon in addition to its own weight.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's own working gives w₂ = 127.4 N − 80 N − 8.82 N = 38.58 N (about 38.6 N), so the balloon can lift about 38.6 N in addition to its own weight, not 41 N.
